questions.question_text:
Consider a network path P—Q—R between nodes P and R via router Q. Node P
sends a file of size 106 bytes to R via this path by splitting the file into chunks of
103 bytes each. Node P sends these chunks one after the other without any wait time
between the successive chunk transmissions. Assume that the size of extra headers
added to these chunks is negligible, and that the chunk size is less than the MTU.

Each of the links P—Q and Q—R has a bandwidth of 106 bits/sec, and negligible
propagation latency. Router Q immediately transmits every packet it receives from
P to R, with negligible processing and queueing delays. Router Q can
simultaneously receive on link P—Q and transmit on link Q—R.

Assume P starts transmitting the chunks at time 𝑡= 0.
Which one of the following options gives the time (in seconds, rounded off to 3
decimal places) at which R receives all the chunks of the file?
questions.subtopic: Concept of layering: OSI and TCP/IP Protocol Stacks
questions.explaination: The file size is $10^6$ bytes split into 1000 chunks of $10^3$ bytes ($8000$ bits) each. Link transmission time for one chunk is $\frac{8000\text{ bits}}{10^6\text{ bps}} = 0.008\text{ s}$. Node P completes sending all 1000 chunks at $t = 1000 \times 0.008 = 8.000\text{ s}$. The last chunk arrives at router Q at $t = 8.000\text{ s}$ and takes another $0.008\text{ s}$ to reach R over link Q---R, completing at $8.008\text{ s}$.

Consider the following grammar 𝐺, with 𝑆 as the start symbol. The grammar 𝐺 has
three incomplete productions denoted by (1), (2), and (3).
𝑆→𝑑𝑎𝑇 | (1)
𝑇→𝑎𝑆 | 𝑏𝑇 | (2)
𝑅→ (3) | 𝜖
The set of terminals is {𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐, 𝑑, 𝑓}. The FIRST and FOLLOW sets of the different
non-terminals are as follows.
FIRST(𝑆) = {𝑐, 𝑑, 𝑓}, FIRST(𝑇) = {𝑎, 𝑏, 𝜖}, FIRST(𝑅) = {𝑐, 𝜖}
FOLLOW(𝑆) = FOLLOW(𝑇) = {𝑐, 𝑓, $}, FOLLOW(𝑅) = {𝑓}
Which one of the following options CORRECTLY fills in the incomplete
productions?
questions.explaination: Since $\text{FIRST}(S) = \{c, d, f\}$ and $S \to daT$ generates $d$, production (1) must generate $c$ and $f$. With (1) as $S \to Rf$ where $\text{FIRST}(R) = \{c, \epsilon\}$, $\text{FIRST}(Rf) = \{c, f\}$. Since $\epsilon \in \text{FIRST}(T)$, production (2) must be $T \to \epsilon$. Production (3) as $R \to cTR$ matches $\text{FIRST}(R) = \{c, \epsilon\}$ and $\text{FOLLOW}(R) = \{f\}$, matching option (A).

questions.question_text:
Consider the following two threads T1 and T2 that update two shared variables
a and b. Assume that initially a = b = 1. Though context switching between
threads can happen at any time, each statement of T1 or T2 is executed atomically
without interruption.
T1 T2
a = a + 1; b = 2 * b;
b = b + 1; a = 2 * a;
Which one of the following options lists all the possible combinations of values of
a and b after both T1 and T2 finish execution?
questions.explaination: Initially $a=b=1$. Let statements be $T_1: [S_1: a=a+1, S_2: b=b+1]$ and $T_2: [S_3: b=2b, S_4: a=2a]$. Executing $T_1$ then $T_2$ yields $a=2, b=2 \to b=4, a=4 \implies (4, 4)$. Executing $T_2$ then $T_1$ yields $b=2, a=2 \to a=3, b=3 \implies (3, 3)$. Executing $S_1, S_3, S_4, S_2$ yields $a=2 \to b=2 \to a=4 \to b=3 \implies (4, 3)$. No valid interleaving can produce $(a=3, b=4)$.

following options represents the first three elements in the heapified array?
questions.subtopic: Trees, binary search trees, binary heaps

The maximum element 131 bubbles up to index 1 (root), its left child becomes 111 (index 2), and right child becomes 90 (index 3).

questions.subtopic: Asymptotic worst case time and space complexity
questions.explaination: Dividing $T(n) = \sqrt{n} T(\sqrt{n}) + n$ by $n$ gives $\frac{T(n)}{n} = \frac{T(\sqrt{n})}{\sqrt{n}} + 1$. Defining $S(n) = \frac{T(n)}{n}$ yields $S(n) = S(\sqrt{n}) + 1$. Substituting $n = 2^{2^k}$ gives $S(2^{2^k}) = S(2^{2^{k-1}}) + 1 = \Theta(k) = \Theta(\log \log n)$. Therefore, $T(n) = n S(n) = \Theta(n \log \log n)$.

the underlying array) of the maximum element stored in the heap. The number of
possible values of 𝑘 is
questions.subtopic: Trees, binary search trees, binary heaps

The symbol → indicates functional dependency in the context of a relational
database. Which of the following options is/are TRUE?
questions.explaination: By Armstrong's decomposition axiom, $(X, Y) \to (Z, W)$ implies $(X, Y) \to Z$ (B is TRUE). By Armstrong's transitivity axiom, $X \to Y$ and $Y \to Z$ implies $X \to Z$ (D is TRUE). By pseudotransitivity, $(X, Y) \to Z$ and $W \to Y$ implies $(X, W) \to Z$ (C is TRUE). Decomposing the left-hand side determinant is invalid in general (A is FALSE).

questions.question_text:
Let 𝐺 be a directed graph and 𝑇 a depth first search (DFS) spanning tree in 𝐺 that
is rooted at a vertex 𝑣. Suppose 𝑇 is also a breadth first search (BFS) tree in 𝐺,
rooted at 𝑣. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE for every such graph 𝐺
and tree 𝑇 ?

options.A: There are no back-edges in 𝐺 with respect to the tree 𝑇
options.B: There are no cross-edges in 𝐺 with respect to the tree 𝑇
options.C: There are no forward-edges in 𝐺 with respect to the tree 𝑇
options.D: The only edges in 𝐺 are the edges in 𝑇

questions.subtopic: Graph traversals, minimum spanning trees, shortest paths
questions.explaination: In a BFS tree $T$, any edge $(u, w)$ in $G$ must connect vertices whose BFS levels differ by at most 1 (i.e., $\text{level}(w) \le \text{level}(u) + 1$). A forward-edge in a DFS tree goes from ancestor $u$ to descendant $w$ with $\text{level}(w) \ge \text{level}(u) + 2$. If such an edge existed in $G$, BFS would explore $w$ directly from $u$ at depth $\text{level}(u) + 1$, contradicting the structure of $T$. Hence, no forward-edges can exist in $G$ with respect to $T$ (C is TRUE).
questions.question_text_latex: Let $G$ be a directed graph and $T$ a depth first search (DFS) spanning tree in $G$ that is rooted at a vertex $v$. Suppose $T$ is also a breadth first search (BFS) tree in $G$, rooted at $v$. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE for every such graph $G$ and tree $T$?

options_latex.C: There are no forward-edges in $G$ with respect to the tree $T$
options_latex.D: The only edges in $G$ are the edges in $T$

questions.question_text:
Let 𝐴 be any 𝑛× 𝑚 matrix, where 𝑚 > 𝑛. Which of the following statements is/are
TRUE about the system of linear equations 𝐴𝑥= 0 ?

options.A: There exist at least 𝑚−𝑛 linearly independent solutions to this system
options.B:
There exist 𝑚−𝑛 linearly independent vectors such that every solution is a linear
combination of these vectors
options.C: There exists a non-zero solution in which at least 𝑚−𝑛 variables are 0
options.D: There exists a solution in which at least 𝑛 variables are non-zero

questions.explaination: The solution space of the homogeneous system $Ax = 0$ is the null space of $A$, whose dimension is $\text{nullity}(A) = m - \text{rank}(A)$. Since $\text{rank}(A) \le n$, we have $\text{nullity}(A) \ge m - n$. This guarantees the existence of at least $m - n$ linearly independent solutions (A is TRUE). The nullity can exceed $m-n$ when $\text{rank}(A) < n$, so (B) is not universally true.

options_latex.B: There exist $m-n$ linearly independent vectors such that every solution is a linear combination of these vectors
options_latex.C: There exists a non-zero solution in which at least $m-n$ variables are 0
options_latex.D: There exists a solution in which at least $n$ variables are non-zero

Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?

options.B: States 3 and 4 are distinguishable in 𝑀
options.C: States 2 and 5 are distinguishable in 𝑀

questions.question_text:
The chromatic number of a graph is the minimum number of colours used in a
proper colouring of the graph. Let 𝐺 be any graph with 𝑛 vertices and chromatic
number 𝑘. Which of the following statements is/are always TRUE?

options.A: 𝐺 contains a complete subgraph with 𝑘 vertices
options.B: 𝐺 contains an independent set of size at least 𝑛/𝑘
options.C: 𝐺 contains at least 𝑘(𝑘−1)/2 edges
options.D: 𝐺 contains a vertex of degree at least 𝑘

questions.explaination: A proper $k$-coloring partitions the $n$ vertices into $k$ independent sets. By the Pigeonhole Principle, at least one of these independent sets has size $\ge \lceil n/k \rceil \ge n/k$ (B is TRUE). In addition, every pair of color classes must have at least one edge between them (otherwise those two colors could be merged, yielding a $(k-1)$-coloring), requiring at least $\binom{k}{2} = \frac{k(k-1)}{2}$ edges (C is TRUE).

options_latex.A: $G$ contains a complete subgraph with $k$ vertices
options_latex.B: $G$ contains an independent set of size at least $n/k$
options_latex.D: $G$ contains a vertex of degree at least $k$

questions.question_text:
Consider the operators ◊ and □ defined by 𝑎◊𝑏= 𝑎+ 2𝑏, 𝑎□𝑏= 𝑎𝑏, for positive
integers. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.C: Operator ◊ over the operator □ obeys the distributive law
options.D: Operator □ over the operator ◊ obeys the distributive law

questions.explaination: For $\square$: $a \square b = ab$, which is associative since $(ab)c = a(bc)$ (B is TRUE). Distributivity of $\square$ over $\diamond$: $a \square (b \diamond c) = a(b + 2c) = ab + 2ac$. Comparing with $(a \square b) \diamond (a \square c) = (ab) \diamond (ac) = ab + 2(ac) = ab + 2ac$; both sides match identically, so $\square$ distributes over $\diamond$ (D is TRUE). For $\diamond$: $(a \diamond b) \diamond c = a + 2b + 2c \neq a + 2b + 4c = a \diamond (b \diamond c)$, so $\diamond$ is not associative.

options_latex.C: Operator $\diamond$ over the operator $\square$ obeys the distributive law
options_latex.D: Operator $\square$ over the operator $\diamond$ obeys the distributive law

questions.question_text:
Consider two set-associative cache memory architectures: WBC, which uses the
write back policy, and WTC, which uses the write through policy. Both of them use
the LRU (Least Recently Used) block replacement policy. The cache memory is
connected to the main memory. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.A: A read miss in WBC never evicts a dirty block
options.B:
A read miss in WTC never triggers a write back operation of a cache block to
main memory
options.C: A write hit in WBC can modify the value of the dirty bit of a cache block
options.D:
A write miss in WTC always writes the victim cache block to main memory
before loading the missed block to the cache

questions.subtopic: Memory hierarchy: cache, main memory and secondary storage
questions.explaination: In a write-through cache (WTC), main memory is updated simultaneously on every cache write, meaning cache lines are never dirty and no eviction ever triggers a write-back to memory (B is TRUE). In a write-back cache (WBC), when a clean block receives a write hit, its dirty bit is set from 0 to 1 to indicate modification (C is TRUE).
questions.question_text_latex: Consider two set-associative cache memory architectures: WBC, which uses the write back policy, and WTC, which uses the write through policy. Both of them use the LRU (Least Recently Used) block replacement policy. The cache memory is connected to the main memory. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options_latex.B: A read miss in WTC never triggers a write back operation of a cache block to main memory
options_latex.C: A write hit in WBC can modify the value of the dirty bit of a cache block

questions.question_text:
Consider a 512 GB hard disk with 32 storage surfaces. There are 4096 sectors per
track and each sector holds 1024 bytes of data. The number of cylinders in the hard
disk is _________
questions.subtopic: Memory hierarchy: cache, main memory and secondary storage
questions.explaination: Disk capacity $= 512\text{ GB} = 512 \times 2^{30}\text{ bytes} = 2^{39}$ bytes. One cylinder comprises 32 surfaces $\times 4096$ sectors/track $\times 1024$ bytes/sector $= 2^5 \times 2^{12} \times 2^{10} = 2^{27}$ bytes. Number of cylinders $= \frac{2^{39}}{2^{27}} = 2^{12} = 4096$.

questions.question_text:
The baseline execution time of a program on a 2 GHz single core machine is
100 nanoseconds (ns). The code corresponding to 90% of the execution time can be
fully parallelized. The overhead for using an additional core is 10 ns when running
on a multicore system. Assume that all cores in the multicore system run their share
of the parallelized code for an equal amount of time.
The number of cores that minimize the execution time of the program is ________
questions.explaination: Baseline runtime is $100\text{ ns}$, with $90\text{ ns}$ parallelizable and $10\text{ ns}$ serial. On $p$ cores, the parallel portion takes $\frac{90}{p}\text{ ns}$ with core overhead of $10(p-1)\text{ ns}$. Total execution time $T(p) = 10 + \frac{90}{p} + 10(p-1) = \frac{90}{p} + 10p$. Evaluating: $T(1) = 100\text{ ns}$, $T(2) = 65\text{ ns}$, $T(3) = 60\text{ ns}$, $T(4) = 62.5\text{ ns}$. The time is minimized at $p = 3$ cores.

questions.question_text:
A given program has 25% load/store instructions. Suppose the ideal CPI (cycles per
instruction) without any memory stalls is 2. The program exhibits 2% miss rate on
instruction cache and 8% miss rate on data cache. The miss penalty is 100 cycles.
The speedup (rounded off to two decimal places) achieved with a perfect cache (i.e.,
with NO data or instruction cache misses) is _________
questions.subtopic: Memory hierarchy: cache, main memory and secondary storage
questions.explaination: Total CPI is given by $\text{CPI} = \text{CPI}_{\text{ideal}} + (\text{I-miss rate} \times \text{penalty}) + (\text{Data-instruction fraction} \times \text{D-miss rate} \times \text{penalty}) = 2 + (0.02 \times 100) + (0.25 \times 0.08 \times 100) = 2 + 2 + 2 = 6$. For a perfect cache with no misses, $\text{CPI}_{\text{perfect}} = \text{CPI}_{\text{ideal}} = 2$. Speedup $= \frac{6}{2} = 3.00$.

questions.subtopic: System calls, processes, threads, inter-process communication
questions.explaination: Initially 1 process with $x=3$. Iteration 1 ($x=3$): `fork()` creates 1 child (total 2 processes); both print "hello" (2 prints) and decrement $x$ to 2. Iteration 2 ($x=2$): each of the 2 processes forks (total 4 processes); all 4 print "hello" (4 prints) and decrement $x$ to 1. Iteration 3 ($x=1$): each of the 4 processes forks (total 8 processes); all 8 print "hello" (8 prints) and decrement $x$ to 0, whereupon the loop ends. Total prints $= 2 + 4 + 8 = 14$.

10.1.1.16, 10.1.1.72, 10.1.1.132, 10.1.1.191, and 10.1.1.205 . The number of

questions.subtopic: Routing protocols: shortest path, flooding, distance vector and link state routing

questions.question_text:
Let 𝐺 = (𝑉, Σ, 𝑆, 𝑃) be a context-free grammar in Chomsky Normal Form with
Σ = {𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐} and 𝑉 containing 10 variable symbols including the start
symbol 𝑆. The string 𝑤 = 𝑎30𝑏30𝑐30 is derivable from 𝑆. The number of steps
(application of rules) in the derivation 𝑆→∗𝑤 is _________
questions.explaination: In a Chomsky Normal Form (CNF) grammar, every production is either $A \to BC$ or $A \to a$. Deriving a string of length $n$ requires $n-1$ non-terminal splitting steps ($A \to BC$) followed by $n$ terminal production steps ($A \to a$), totaling $2n-1$ steps. For $w = a^{30}b^{30}c^{30}$, the length is $n = 90$, so the number of derivation steps is $2(90) - 1 = 179$.
questions.question_text_latex: Let $G = (V, \Sigma, S, P)$ be a context-free grammar in Chomsky Normal Form with $\Sigma = \{a, b, c\}$ and $V$ containing 10 variable symbols including the start symbol $S$. The string $w = a^{30}b^{30}c^{30}$ is derivable from $S$. The number of steps (application of rules) in the derivation $S \Rightarrow^* w$ is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\. (Answer in integer)

questions.question_text:
The number of edges present in the forest generated by the DFS traversal of an
undirected graph 𝐺 with 100 vertices is 40. The number of connected components
in 𝐺 is _________
questions.explaination: A DFS traversal of an undirected graph with $V$ vertices and $k$ connected components produces a spanning forest containing $k$ trees. A tree with $v_i$ vertices contains $v_i - 1$ edges, so the total number of tree edges in the forest is $\sum (v_i - 1) = V - k$. Given $V = 100$ and $E = 40$, we have $40 = 100 - k \implies k = 60$ connected components.

questions.question_text:
Consider the following two regular expressions over the alphabet {0,1}:
𝑟= 0∗+ 1∗
𝑠= 01∗+ 10∗
The total number of strings of length less than or equal to 5, which are
neither in 𝑟 nor in 𝑠, is _________
questions.explaination: The total number of binary strings of length $\le 5$ is $\sum_{i=0}^5 2^i = 1+2+4+8+16+32 = 63$. Language $L(r) = 0^* + 1^*$ contains $\epsilon$ and $0^k, 1^k$ for each length $k \in \{1..5\}$ (11 strings). Language $L(s) = 01^* + 10^*$ contains $01^{k-1}$ and $10^{k-1}$ for each length $k \in \{1..5\}$. At $k=1$, $0$ and $1$ overlap with $L(r)$; for $k \in \{2..5\}$, the $4 \times 2 = 8$ strings are disjoint from $L(r)$. Thus, $|L(r) \cup L(s)| = 11 + 8 = 19$. The number of strings in neither language is $63 - 19 = 44$.

questions.question_text:
Consider a memory management system that uses a page size of 2 KB. Assume that
both the physical and virtual addresses start from 0. Assume that the pages 0, 1, 2,
and 3 are stored in the page frames 1, 3, 2, and 0, respectively. The physical address
(in decimal format) corresponding to the virtual address 2500 (in decimal format)
is _________
questions.explaination: With page size $2\text{ KB} = 2048\text{ bytes}$, virtual address $2500$ has virtual page number $\lfloor 2500 / 2048 \rfloor = 1$ and offset $2500 \pmod{2048} = 452$. Page 1 maps to frame 3. The physical address is $(\text{frame } 3 \times 2048) + \text{offset } 452 = 6144 + 452 = 6596$.

questions.question_text:
A bag contains 10 red balls and 15 blue balls. Two balls are drawn randomly without
replacement. Given that the first ball drawn is red, the probability (rounded off to 3
decimal places) that both balls drawn are red is _________
questions.explaination: Let $R_1, R_2$ be the events of drawing red balls on the first and second draws without replacement. The conditional probability that both are red given the first is red is $P(R_1 \cap R_2 \mid R_1) = P(R_2 \mid R_1)$. Given that 1 red ball is already drawn, 9 red balls remain out of $9 + 15 = 24$ total balls, so $P(R_2 \mid R_1) = \frac{9}{24} = \frac{3}{8} = 0.375$.

questions.question_text:
Consider sending an IP datagram of size 1420 bytes (including 20 bytes of IP
header) from a sender to a receiver over a path of two links with a router between
them. The first link (sender to router) has an MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit)
size of 542 bytes, while the second link (router to receiver) has an MTU size of 360
bytes. The number of fragments that would be delivered at the receiver is ________
questions.subtopic: Fragmentation and IP addressing, IPv4, CIDR notation
questions.explaination: The datagram has 20 bytes IP header and 1400 bytes data. Link 1 has $\text{MTU} = 542$ bytes (max data per fragment is $\lfloor (542-20)/8 \rfloor \times 8 = 520$ bytes), producing 3 fragments with data sizes 520, 520, and 360 bytes. Link 2 has $\text{MTU} = 360$ bytes (max data is $\lfloor (360-20)/8 \rfloor \times 8 = 336$ bytes). At router Q, fragment 1 (520 bytes) is fragmented into 2 ($336 + 184$), fragment 2 (520 bytes) is fragmented into 2 ($336 + 184$), and fragment 3 (360 bytes) is fragmented into 2 ($336 + 24$). Total fragments delivered at the receiver $= 2 + 2 + 2 = 6$.
